title: Rolling It Out to a Team — Module Quiz

items.q: Why is a tool that works not the same as a tool that is adopted?
options: Working tools are rarely well designed
People already have a way of working, the first experience decides, and nobody has spare time to learn something new
Adoption depends mainly on the price of the tool
items.explain: A tool has to beat what people already do, in their hands, on a busy day. A poor first answer ends the trial, usually permanently.

items.q: Which question produces the most honest picture of someone's work?
options: Would you find AI useful for this task?
Walk me through the last time you did this
How much time do you think this takes per week?
items.explain: People describe real work honestly and give polite guesses to hypothetical preferences.

items.q: Someone says reports take too long, but watching shows the writing takes twenty minutes and the rest is chasing numbers. What follows?
options: A faster writing tool will solve the problem
The named problem is not the real one, and a tool that writes faster saves nothing that matters
The person is exaggerating how long reports take
items.explain: Keep asking what happens next until you reach a step someone would pay to avoid. That step is the candidate.

items.q: What is the honest base rate for a tool built and handed to a team?
options: Most colleagues adopt it after a demonstration
The author uses it and nobody else does, unless the work was understood first
Adoption depends mainly on how well the tool is designed
items.explain: Colleagues have their own habits and did not ask for it. Starting from their real problem is what changes the odds.

items.q: Why include a sceptic in a pilot group?
options: Sceptics are easier to convince and then convert others
Their objections are the ones the wider team will raise later, and hearing them early is valuable
It keeps the group size balanced
items.explain: A willing sceptic is worth several enthusiasts. Enthusiasts forgive a great deal and will tell you it is wonderful.

items.q: Why write the success and failure criteria before a pilot starts?
options: Regulators require written criteria
It is hard to see your own work fail, and a criterion written beforehand cannot be adjusted to fit the result
It shortens the pilot
items.explain: Without it, every result gets read as success by the person who built the thing.

items.q: Why is choosing an easy task for a pilot a trap?
options: Easy tasks produce too little data
It gives a good result that vanishes on contact with real work
Participants find easy tasks boring
items.explain: A pilot task should be representative of the actual work, not flattering to the tool.

items.q: Which four properties make a good pilot task?
options: Urgent, high-value, complex and unusual
Frequent, low-stakes, checkable and representative
Cheap, quick, popular and new
items.explain: Frequent enough to produce data, low-stakes so mistakes are annoying not harmful, checkable quickly, and typical of the real work.

items.q: Why are tool-specific tutorials a poor use of training time?
options: Tools are too simple to need training
Interfaces change every few weeks, while a habit of checking output works on any tool
Participants prefer theory
items.explain: A screen-by-screen walk-through is out of date almost at once, and it teaches people to follow steps rather than notice wrong output.

items.q: What is the most useful way to tell a team what not to paste into a tool?
options: A general instruction to be careful with personal information
A short list of concrete examples tied to their own data
A long policy document to read before first use
items.explain: People reason from cases better than from principles. Customer names, account numbers and HR files are examples they can recognise.

items.q: Why include a deliberate failure in training?
options: To discourage people from using the tool
Seeing it fail in a way that looks right is more persuasive than being told it can
Failures are easier to demonstrate than successes
items.explain: A failure drawn from the team's own area is best. It builds the checking habit that matters most.

items.q: Why make it safe for people to say they do not know how the tool works?
options: It reduces the number of questions asked
Mistakes people fear to admit never reach you, and you cannot fix what you cannot see
It shortens training sessions
items.explain: Treat errors found by checking as the system working. If someone catches the tool being wrong, the right response is thanks.

items.q: What typically happens when an organisation bans AI tools outright?
options: Use stops completely
Use continues out of sight on personal accounts, so you lose the ability to advise on or protect against it
Productivity rises because people focus on other work
items.explain: Shadow use has every risk of the sanctioned version plus the one that you cannot see it. A policy that steers beats one that forbids.

items.q: Why name the plan, and not only the tool, in an acceptable-use note?
options: Plans determine how fast the tool responds
Data terms can differ sharply between a business account and a free personal one
Plans decide which features are visible
items.explain: 'Use the company account, not a personal one' can be the most protective line on the page.

items.q: Who is accountable for work produced with a tool?
options: The tool's vendor
The person who uses the tool and sends the result on
Whoever approved the tool
items.explain: 'The tool wrote it' is not an answer to a customer or a regulator. Saying so in advance removes ambiguity about who owns a mistake.

items.q: Someone asks whether the tool will take their job and you do not know. What is the strongest response?
options: Assure them it will not, to calm the situation
Say what you know, what you do not, and what you commit to, with specifics you can keep
Change the subject to the benefits of the tool
items.explain: A reassurance that is later found false discounts everything you said. Honest uncertainty with a concrete commitment is believed.

items.q: Why is a quality concern from the people doing the work worth treating as expertise?
options: It usually means they dislike the tool
They know where the subtle mistakes live, and their failure cases make the best test set
Quality concerns can be ignored once training is complete
items.explain: People who contribute the cases tend to become the ones who make it work, because they have a stake in its being right.

items.q: Why is secretly tracking individual usage a risk?
options: Usage data is too inaccurate to be useful
It is discovered sooner or later, and the damage to trust far outweighs the value of the data
Platforms prohibit exporting usage data
items.explain: If you measure, say so and say why. Aggregate numbers to learn whether the tool helps are reasonable; ranking people by use is not.

items.q: Why take a baseline before a pilot?
options: Baselines are required to purchase a licence
Without a measurement of how the work went before, any improvement is a feeling
Baselines make the pilot run faster
items.explain: Measure the task as it is done now, and measure it the same way afterwards.

items.q: Why can a tool that drafts in a minute fail to save any time?
options: Drafting speed is irrelevant to productivity
Writing the request, reading, checking and fixing can take longer than the draft saved
Drafts are always shorter than hand-written text
items.explain: A tool that produces a draft in one minute and needs fifteen to verify has not saved fourteen. Count the whole of the work.

items.q: Why is login or active-user count weak evidence that a tool helped?
options: Counts are rarely recorded accurately
It measures activity and compliance, not benefit, since a tool people are told to use will be used
Platforms do not release usage data
items.explain: Heavy use may mean the tool is hard to get right. Measure outcomes such as time, corrections and errors.

items.q: Why show a rate as unknown, not zero, when there is no data behind it?
options: Zero is mathematically undefined
A zero reads as 'nothing is wrong' when it actually means 'nothing is known'
Unknown values load faster
items.explain: A measure with no data behind it must not look like good news.

items.q: Why are reported failures described as a gift?
options: They show that the users are paying attention
Each is a real input from a real task where the tool failed, and a test case that cost nothing
They reduce the support team's workload
items.explain: Put each in the test set with a note of what it broke, so that an escape which is fixed does not return unrecorded.

items.q: What does a short running log of changes do?
options: Satisfies a regulatory requirement
Shows the thing is being tended, explains changes in behaviour, and makes 'it used to work' answerable
Replaces the need for version control
items.explain: Two lines per change is enough. It is also searchable when someone reports that something has got worse.

items.q: What is the commonest way a rollout ends?
options: A dramatic failure that forces it to be withdrawn
A quiet fade, with people returning to the old way without announcing it
A formal decision by management to cancel it
items.explain: Nobody complains because nobody is invested. The guard is to look: check use and satisfaction at intervals and treat a decline as information.

items.q: What is the commonest reason a rollout fails to take?
options: People resist all change
It solved a problem the team did not feel they had
The tool was too expensive
items.explain: They were asked to adopt a solution to a difficulty they did not have. Ask what the hardest part of their week is.

items.q: Why is blaming users for non-adoption unhelpful?
options: Users are rarely at fault
It ends the investigation, since if the fault is theirs there is nothing to find
It may cause legal difficulties
items.explain: Ask what you would have to believe for their behaviour to be reasonable. Usually there is a version of that sentence you can complete.

items.q: Why is effort already spent not a reason to continue a failing rollout?
options: The effort cannot be measured
That effort is gone either way; the only question is whether continuing is worth the cost from here
Continuing always costs more than stopping
items.explain: Pressure not to withdraw is strongest when you built the thing, which is when your judgement is least reliable. Ask someone who did not.
